title: Gianni v. R. Russel & Co., Inc.
summary: A tenant could not prove a separate oral promise of exclusive soft-drink sales where the written lease appeared complete and already addressed what he could sell.
notes:
The court's much-quoted statement of the rule: "Where parties, without any fraud or mistake, have deliberately put their engagements in writing, the law declares the writing to be not only the best, but the only evidence of their agreement." (Gianni v. R. Russell & Co., 281 Pa. 320, 126 A. 791 (1924)).

The test the court applied: if the subject of the alleged oral agreement is one that would naturally and normally have been included in the written contract, evidence of the oral agreement is inadmissible to add to or vary the writing absent fraud, accident or mistake.

sections.Parties: Gianni operated a shop in a Pittsburgh office building. R. Russel & Company acquired the building and leased the shop to him. He sought damages for breach of an asserted oral exclusivity promise.
sections.Material Facts: The shop sold tobacco, fruit, candy, and soft drinks. During negotiations for a new three-year lease, Gianni claimed that he agreed to stop selling tobacco and pay higher rent in return for the exclusive right to sell soft drinks in the building. The written lease addressed the permitted use and merchandise but contained no exclusivity promise. After the lease was signed, an adjoining room was rented to a drug company that also sold soft drinks, allegedly reducing his receipts and profits. He offered evidence of oral assurances given before, and allegedly repeated at, execution. The landlord’s representative denied making them.
sections.Procedural History: Gianni recovered at trial on the asserted oral agreement. In 1924 the Pennsylvania Supreme Court reversed and entered judgment for the landlord. The court treated the scope and completeness of the writing as a legal question.
sections.Issue: Could the tenant enforce the oral exclusivity promise as an independent collateral agreement outside the written lease?
sections.Holding: No. The promise concerned a subject embraced by the complete written lease and would naturally have been included in it. The parol evidence rule excluded the asserted oral agreement.
sections.Reasoning:
The court asked whether similarly situated parties would naturally and normally put the claimed oral undertaking into the same writing. The lease already regulated the shop’s sales, including the tenant’s promise to stop selling tobacco. The alleged exclusivity right was closely connected to that restriction and to the same consideration. Its subject was therefore within the writing’s scope.

Calling the promise an independent oral contract could not avoid the rule when the very subject was dealt with in the writing. The plaintiff expressly disclaimed fraud, accident, and mistake, so the court did not confront the grounds on which reformation or another exception might have been available. The result concerns the effect of an integrated writing, not an evidentiary finding that nobody ever uttered the oral assurance.

textbookImport.basis: Paraphrase of the exact supplied Fall 2026 Contracts Supplement; no subsequent-treatment review.

learning.why: Gianni supplies the restrictive “naturally included” approach. Compare Masterson’s contextual approach to a collateral term and TeeVee Toons’ CISG analysis of the parties’ intent.

topics.assent: The issue is what the parties adopted as their final agreement.
topics.parol-evidence: Excludes an oral promise within the scope of an apparently complete writing.
topics.interpretation: Uses the written treatment of merchandise restrictions to identify the scope of integration.
topics.integration: The dispositive question was whether the lease was a complete integration covering the subject of the alleged oral promise, so the case is the standard illustration of the integration inquiry.

mnemonic.rationale: A storeroom lease and an oral promise
